newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Madelin set to win party power base.
newsitem.headline: France's Madelin set to win party power base.

text.p: France's free-marketeer ex-finance minister Alain Madelin was set to win the leadership of the opposition Republican Party (PR) on Tuesday, giving him a power base if he can widen the divided group beset by legal problems.

With his chances of a new government role in tatters after the left's upset victory in this month's parliamentary election, Madelin hopes to turn the right-wing group into a broad liberal party to vie for power in the next election, by 2002.

"I now feel in a position to rally and re-build the big liberal family...I have a great ambition for it: to put it in a position to lead the next (government) changeover and make it a success," he told the conservative daily Le Figaro.

Madelin, 51, looked certain to be elected president of the PR at a national congress in the Paris suburb of Levallois later in the day, although some colleagues accused him of trying to stage a coup and leave them to endorse a fait accompli.
"Vanquished generals are sharing out the spoils, this is unprecedented," said Gilles de Robien who put up a last-minute challenge to Madelin in order, he said, to preserve democracy within the party.

De Robien presented his moderate challenge to what he called Madelin's "ultra-liberal" views through a paid advertisement in Le Figaro because he said the party had withheld its mailing list from him until it was too late to write to members.

Ex-defence minister Francois Leotard agreed to give up the presidency of the PR, which Madelin plans to re-name Liberal Democracy, while staying on as leader of the centre-right's umbrella group, the Union for French Democracy (UDF).

The PR leadership would give Madelin the power base he has lacked throughout his chequered career. Three times a cabinet member, he was sacked as finance minister after only a few months in 1995 for attacking civil servants' privileges.
The PR congress is part of a series of moves to reorganise a shaken right, stunned by its unexpected election fiasco.

The UDF's senior partner in opposition, the Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) founded by President Jacques Chirac, will also change leaders at a July 6 congress after ex-prime minister Alain Juppe was forced to step down following the poll disaster.
Socially-minded Gaullist Philippe Seguin is set to take over the party in alliance with supporters of former prime minister Edouard Balladur, Chirac's unsuccessful presidential challenger.
Chirac briefly anointed an unlikely duo of Seguin and Madelin as the right's standard bearers last month in a doomed last-minute bid to stave off defeat after Juppe's withdrawal.

Madelin says he wants to unite all economic liberals who are now scattered among other parties, and win back disgruntled conservative voters who have deserted mainstream parties and gone over to the far-right, anti-immigrant National Front.
The Front polled 15 percent and the right needs to reconquer some of its supporters to stand a chance of returning to power.
Madelin faces a hard task rebuilding a party still reeling from a rift in the 1995 presidential election when most of its leaders backed the loser, Balladur. Madelin backed Chirac.
The PR, which is the second largest group in the UDF and claims 33,000 members, is also beset by financial and legal problems.

Its coffers are reported to be almost empty, and it is under investigation on suspicion of illicit funding involving cash deposits of millions of francs (dollars) channelled through offshore bank accounts and front companies in Panama, Luxembourg and Switzerland.
